title: A Missile That Runs on a Tiny Nuclear Reactor? Yep, and It's Flying Over the Arctic!
summary: Imagine a missile that can fly for hours and hours, looping around in the sky like a bird. That's what Russia tested last October above the Arctic Circle. The missile is called Burevestnik, or Skyfall, and it's powered by a small nuclear reactor—a tiny engine that uses atomic energy. Two scientists from MIT, Jake Hecla and R. Scott Kemp, studied videos and figured out how it works. They think the missile sucks air right through its nuclear core to heat it up and shoot it out the back. That's very different from most nuclear reactors, which keep the dangerous radiation sealed inside. But this design probably spews radiation as it flies. Hecla says anyone near the test site could be in "enormous risk." The missile is about the size of a big cruise missile, flying as fast as a passenger plane—around 575 miles per hour. Because it's nuclear-powered, it could stay in the air almost forever, waiting to strike from any direction. The U.S. tried building nuclear missiles in the 1960s but stopped because they were too dangerous. Now Russia's test might start a new and scary arms race. "This is something that is possible, but wildly expensive and very dangerous," Hecla says.
why_it_matters: This matters because if a missile leaks radiation, it could harm people and animals wherever it flies, and it might spark a race to build even scarier weapons.

The Arctic Circle is a large, icy area around the North Pole where Russia test-fires many missiles safely away from towns.
MIT (the Massachusetts Institute of Technology) is a university where scientists like Jake Hecla and R. Scott Kemp study difficult engineering problems.
